newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico 1997 monetary plan seen as balm to recovery.
newsitem.headline: Mexico 1997 monetary plan seen as balm to recovery.

text.p: Mexico's 1997 monetary policy plan is a part of an overall conservative policy mix that should help the economic recovery by allowing the peso to carefully depreciate, economists said on Thursday.

"It's the right policy mix to facilitate the recovery and prevent additional real appreciation of the peso, which would hurt export competitiveness," said Lehman Bros economist Darryl McLeod of the plan, which was released Wednesday.

Bears Stearns & Co economist David Malpass added: "It is a logical continuation of the monetary policy they have pursued in 1996, and I think that it will allow the peso to weaken gradually in stair-steps."
Current monetary policy aims to limit inflationary pressure by controlling growth in the money supply.
The main point of the monetary program released on Wednesday is an approximate 24.5 percent increase in the monetary base -- basically coins and bills -- during 1997 from the year before.
The central bank also plans to increase net international assets by at least $1.9 billion during 1997.
Banco de Mexico declined to give a target for the peso when it gave the broad outlines of its monetary plan for next year.
Central bank officials say that in a free-floating regime such as Mexico has, there is neither an interest rate nor an exchange rate target.
But analysts say that the overall policy mix in Mexico is one that aims at an orderly depreciation of the peso to keep the real exchange rate in line with that of its North American partners.
"It (the peso) weakens becuase that is one of the goals of monetary policy, a convergence of the real exchange rates of the U.S., Mexico and Canada," Malpass said.
In its budget planning, the Finance Ministry has set out an assumed average 1997 exchange rate of 8.53 per dollar. The peso closed Wednesday at 7.9070/7.9110.

In periods of sharp volatility, the central bank will tighten liquidity in money markets which drives up interest rates and supports the peso, but officials bristle at any suggestion of a target for the currency.
A stronger peso could hurt the incipient economic recovery, economists said.
"What you don't want going into a recovery like this is strong growth to drive up real interest rates, and that to drive up the peso because you set yourself up for a problem," McLeod said.

"The plan is a nice combination of accumulating dollars and slightly increasing the supply of pesos to accomodate increased money demand and to prevent interest rates from increasing during a strong recovery," he said.
In its plan, the central bank has also made clear that it will not provide more liquidity than is required in its open market operations.

"Although this might be a legitimate monetary policy tool under certain conditions, a net positive liquidity position (even if slight) would send a negative message, especially in an election year, that monetary policy is expansionary," said Valores Finamex economist Ann Ginsburg in a report.
